about: Every claim this project makes about itself, with the state of the thing claimed, where its numbers came from, and the file that proves it. The two state vocabularies are the ones in src/model/capability.ts and nowhere else, so a state cannot appear here that the interface pages do not also know. Checked by tests/unit/claims.test.ts, which fails if a state is invented, an id repeats, or an evidence path does not exist on disk.
null_data_means: Some claims are about the shape of this repository rather than about a measurement it displays. Those carry data: null and a why_no_data line, because stretching a data state to cover them would make the vocabulary mean less. See DECISIONS.md D-059.

claims.claim: HydraDB v0.1.1 is built from source and serves this project over its HTTP query API on loopback.
claims.reproduce: bash scripts/hydra-node.sh start && bash scripts/hydra-node.sh status
claims.caveat: The node runs on this machine and is the native Cypher proof. Production does not replay this node or host it: the deployed adapter reads deterministic addressed records from HydraDB Cloud, then Lacuna applies temporal and relationship resolution in application code.

claims.claim: Production stores collection-scoped sources and graph-shaped entity records in HydraDB Cloud, fetches deterministic addressed records for each answer, and applies temporal standing, contradiction, abstention and multi-hop resolution in Lacuna code.
claims.reproduce: npm run ingest:cloud && npm run parity:cloud
claims.caveat: HydraDB Cloud supplies persistent addressed records, semantic query and extracted relations. It does not execute Lacuna's current/superseded or contradiction policy. The separate self-hosted NodeSource executes native Cypher; that genuine proof is not the deployed Cloud answer path.

claims.claim: Which Cypher this engine accepts was established by running 162 probes against a live node, not by reading a compatibility table.
claims.caveat: Each record holds the query, the parameters, the HTTP status and the engine's own rejection text, unedited. The unsupported list in the integration doc is derived from these files rather than assumed.

claims.claim: The generated corpus loads into the graph as vertices and edges, and a second run adds nothing.

measured.counted_by: npm run census, which reported: graph matches the plan exactly

claims.reproduce: npm run ingest && npm run census
claims.caveat: The counts are today's, from the census. The timings are from the 2026-08-13 run, when the same pipeline moved 5,642 vertices and 5,705 edges, and they are left at what was measured rather than scaled to the larger corpus. The corpus is generated by this repository. It is a synthetic workplace history with known answers, which is what makes the evaluation checkable, and it is not anybody's real messages.

claims.claim: The verdict on a question is decided from explicit claim relationships and temporal fields. No model reads the stored text on the deterministic Ask path.
claims.caveat: Deterministic means the same stored claim records give the same verdict, not that the verdict is right about the world. On the self-hosted adapter those records come from native Cypher reads; on production Cloud they come from addressed inspect reads and Lacuna performs the resolution. What the verdict is right about is the generated corpus, which is what the evaluation measures.

claims.claim: Over 64 questions covering nine kinds of thread, every answer matched the expected one.
claims.caveat: 64 questions over one generated corpus. A hundred per cent on a set this size is a statement about this corpus and this question set, not a general accuracy figure. The four blast-radius cases use known generated subjects and the evaluation API; they do not prove the exact 399-character package-session request or a general Web, CLI or MCP blast command.

claims.claim: When the graph does not support an answer, the system says which of the five absences it is instead of answering.
claims.caveat: Same 64 question set as the evaluation claim. The five absences are named in the interface, and each one points at the read that came back empty.

claims.claim: Against five flat retrieval approaches over 51 configurations, no configuration matches this system on correctness. The closest, hybrid retrieval with two hop expansion and conflict handling at a cut-off of 50, comes one question short.
claims.caveat: The lead is one question, and is written as one question everywhere it appears. Nothing here claims better recall or better abstention: the closest rival matches this system on both, with the same zero unsupported answers. What the run does separate is context size, 18 tokens against 1,843, and a graph read that returns the claim rather than the passages around it.

claims.claim: The unit suite covers the renderer, the resolver, the decoders, the voice machine, the CLI, the MCP adapter and this file, and it needs no database.
claims.caveat: Negative paths are asserted, so the run prints handled errors to stderr on purpose. A green summary line with error text above it is the expected shape.

claims.claim: The contract suite runs against the live node and fails if the wire shape or the Cypher subset moves.
claims.reproduce: bash scripts/hydra-node.sh start && npm run test:contract
claims.caveat: These skip rather than pass when no node is reachable. A run that reports skips is not a run that passed.

claims.claim: A fresh clone installs, typechecks, tests, ingests and answers, recorded end to end.
claims.caveat: The clone reads a local .env.local for its HydraDB token, so the transcript ends with an instruction to delete the clone.

claims.claim: The screenshot set is produced by one command against the running server, at three viewports plus full page, and every file is read back off disk and checked before the run is allowed to pass.
claims.caveat: Every image is a capture of this build serving the seeded corpus. None is a mockup and none was retouched. One capture asks Chrome for a light preference and comes back byte identical to its dark twin, because the page has one ground. See DECISIONS.md D-052 and D-059.

claims.claim: The package declares two runtime dependencies: the official MCP SDK, and hash-wasm for content hashing. Neither is on the answer path.
claims.why_no_data: This is a fact about package.json, not a measurement the product displays.
claims.caveat: This said one dependency until 2026-08-19. A second was added and the entry was not updated, which is the failure mode a claims ledger exists to prevent, so it is recorded rather than silently corrected.

claims.claim: The local HTML server at src/view ships no script, and serves default-src 'none' to say so. The deployed product is a React application and does ship one: a single same-origin bundle, under a Content-Security-Policy of script-src 'self'.
claims.why_no_data: This is a fact about what the server emits, not a measurement.
claims.reproduce:
npm run serve  # then: curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:3014/ | grep -i content-security-policy
curl -sI https://lacuna-five.vercel.app/ | grep -i content-security-policy
claims.caveat: This entry read 'No page ships a script' until 2026-08-19, which was true of the HTML server it was written about and false of the deployment after the React cutover. The two are different servers and the claim now says which one it is about.

claims.claim: The voice interface and provider routes exist, with explicit listening, thinking, speaking, interrupted, error and typed-fallback states. Current production has server-side ElevenLabs configuration and a live provider-backed token/audio boundary; microphone/STT and browser playback acceptance remain separate gates.
claims.reproduce: npm test && npm run serve  # then open /voice
claims.caveat: The production smoke proves a real server-issued provider token and bounded MPEG audio response without printing secrets. It does not prove microphone capture, provider transcription, browser autoplay acceptance or interruption in a human browser session.

claims.claim: Realtime speech-to-text code targets ElevenLabs Scribe through a server-issued single-use token; it is fixture-tested and configured for production, but lacks an accepted live microphone/provider session.
claims.caveat: No production microphone or provider session has been accepted. Configuration presence is not proof of working speech recognition.

claims.claim: Text-to-speech code streams ElevenLabs audio through the server with cancellation and backpressure, and the deployed provider boundary returns real bounded MPEG audio; browser playback remains an owner-session gate.
claims.caveat: The smoke proves provider audio at the HTTP boundary, not that a specific browser accepted autoplay or that a person heard the clip. The film narration remains a separate artifact.

claims.claim: Production voice keeps provider credentials server-side and retains typed Ask as a fallback; native-first playback and provider routes are implemented, with the live TTS boundary verified and browser/STT acceptance still pending.
claims.reproduce: open /voice on production and request provider speech
claims.caveat: The live smoke proves provider readiness and server audio, but a real production STT/TTS/interruption session in the owner's browser is still required.

claims.claim: The deterministic Ask and retrieval path calls no language model. The separate governed agent runtime can call a configured Groq-compatible model for Researcher and Reviewer stages.
claims.caveat: The no-model claim applies only to Ask and the resolver. One production agent run proves a bounded two-role flow, not arbitrary models, arbitrary agents or an autonomous general-purpose agent platform.

claims.claim: Password-account persistence has historical production proof, while the current hosted release deliberately refuses new password accounts and requires Google for signup.
claims.caveat: The 12/12 password run is historical proof for an existing password account, not a current signup path. Hosted password creation is disabled because the HydraDB document boundary cannot atomically enforce a unique email. Existing password identities remain isolated from Google identities.

claims.claim: The deployed Google sign-in boundary uses provider/subject binding, signed-token verification, request-bound PKCE S256 and state, nonce binding, isolated overlapping attempts, hardened cookies and non-cacheable redirects; its production security gate passed 16/16 and an authorized browser completed the provider callback.
claims.caveat: The browser proof uses the already-authorized owner identity and does not claim a different Google identity was created or that account ownership was transferred. Legacy unbound Google records fail closed.

claims.claim: Two built-in no-write roles can persist a bounded Researcher to Reviewer run with lifecycle, Context Pack, evidence, verdict and timing.
claims.caveat: This is not an arbitrary user-created agent platform. CLI and MCP do not expose lifecycle commands. The latest accepted run was produced after removing a hand-written predicate subset that had omitted `runbook_owner`; it now carries both conflicting claims and no authoritative writeback. Accepted public records are inspectable, but production does not allow anonymous visitors to create a persisted run.

claims.claim: Production makes the public preview read-only: anonymous explore/demo agent-run POSTs return 403, while the signed-in CSRF-protected workspace route still creates and persists real workspace-scoped runs.
claims.caveat: The accepted public run records remain readable. NO_WRITE means no authoritative memory mutation; a run record itself is operational state, which is why anonymous creation fails closed. Production probes covered both public route names; a new signed-in issue/run session was not created during this gate.

claims.claim: The public catalogue exposes seven redacted connector descriptors. Private workflows are implemented for one-off file ingestion, public GitHub snapshot import, public HTTPS/API import, and signed bounded webhook delivery; workspace observations remain authenticated.
claims.reproduce: npm run smoke:demo -- https://lacuna-five.vercel.app && npx vitest run tests/unit/connectors-api.test.ts tests/unit/demo-api.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
claims.caveat: Available means the workflow is implemented and deployment-supported; it does not mean a user's workspace is connected or syncing. Private imports still require sign-in and CSRF, and the webhook secret is revealed only once. GitLab, Linear, Jira, Slack, Notion, Gmail, Confluence, Database source and Spotify are not implemented.

claims.claim: The exact 399-character package-session blast-radius request is NOT_PROVEN by the shipped Web, agent, MCP or CLI surfaces.
claims.reproduce: Inspect artifacts/verification/2026-08-21-v10/package-session-proof-audit.json and repeat its listed Web, agent, MCP and CLI probes.
claims.caveat: This negative verdict is about that exact subject and full workflow. It does not negate the four generated gold blast-radius evaluation cases, the in-process pact-check proof, or the fixed tenant-router impact comparison; none of those exposes the requested arbitrary cross-channel blast workflow.

claims.claim: Daily schedule definitions and dispatch claims persist, but hosted execution is not distributed exactly-once.
claims.caveat: The file adapter serializes within one process. The HydraDB adapter has no compare-and-swap or transaction seam, so idempotency, quota and lease decisions are not atomic across simultaneous Vercel instances. Vercel Hobby cadence is daily and imprecise within the selected hour.

claims.claim: Private MCP uses signed-in CSRF-protected issue/revoke routes, a 256-bit random bearer stored digest-only, cross-workspace refusal, bounded streamed bodies and rate-limited calls.
claims.reproduce: npx vitest run tests/unit/mcp-capability-store.test.ts tests/unit/mcp-http.test.ts tests/unit/mcp-capability-api.test.ts
claims.caveat: Production correctly rejected the installed legacy version-1 ChatGPT capability after the security migration. A signed-in owner must mint a version-2 capability before production issue/use/revoke can be accepted. Process-local rate limits are not a distributed quota. Public MCP is the verified remote surface.

claims.claim: The ChatGPT Lacuna app called the production public MCP health, ask, timeline, explain, sentence-read, search and fetch tools against HydraDB Cloud.
claims.reproduce: Connect ChatGPT developer mode to https://lacuna-five.vercel.app/mcp and repeat the seven calls listed in the evidence JSON.
claims.caveat: This is a read-only public-corpus ChatGPT proof. It is not a Claude proof and not a private `lacuna_remember` proof. The installed private connector still holds a legacy capability and must be reminted.

claims.claim: A metadata-verified 179-second historical V8 MP4 exists with the Vaibhav Lalwani Professional narration and burned-in sentence captions; the owner rejected it and it is not submission media.
claims.reproduce: Inspect artifacts/video/final-metadata.json and run Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 video/hyperframes/renders/lacuna-v8-judges-master-vaibhav.mp4
claims.caveat: The artifact is retained only as historical V8 evidence. It must not be uploaded, described as a V10 candidate, or used as a fallback submission master. The clean clone MP3 is local and gitignored to avoid redistributing biometric source audio; its hash, duration, model and generation recipe remain recorded. The burned-in captions use deterministic sentence timing and the matching SRT ends at 00:02:57,398.

claims.claim: The MCP server speaks the protocol over stdio and over Streamable HTTP, to clients written here and to one that was not. The parity script's SDK client drives both transports end to end, and the MCP Inspector CLI at 2.2.0, a separate codebase, consumed the documented mcpServers config block, spawned the server through it, listed the tools and called lacuna_ask and lacuna_health over stdio, then listed and called again over HTTP. The two tools/list responses are byte-identical across transports and the answered values match the parity sweep.
claims.reproduce: npm run parity   # both transports end to end; the inspector commands are in the 2026-08-14e README
claims.caveat: This verifies the public read surface. The third-party client is MCP Inspector's CLI, not ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor or an agent host. Private capability issuance and production wiring remain a separate partial claim. The parity script's HTTP session uses the official SDK Client and validates each outputSchema, which proves protocol/schema conformance rather than named-host compatibility.

claims.claim: The command line answers from the same live graph and prints the same typed result as JSON, both when a current claim exists and when the graph never stated one.
claims.caveat: The JSON caps evidence at fifty items and reports the true count in evidenceTotal. Nothing is published to a package registry, and the CLI does not expose agent create, run, cancel, retry or schedule lifecycle commands.

claims.claim: MCP over stdio, MCP over its HTTP transport, and the command line return the same value for the same question, across all sixty-four gold questions from the evaluation plus two deep cases: same status, answer, reason code, claim id, superseded claims, evidence, evidence total, source state, and same set of graph reads with the same parameters and row counts.
claims.caveat: The check proves Lacuna CLI and both MCP transports agree, not that the answers are right and not that ChatGPT or Claude connected. The order of concurrent reads is excluded. The two MCP surfaces share one tool implementation, so HTTP exercises the transport rather than a second answer implementation.

claims.claim: A copy of the product is public at https://lacuna-five.vercel.app. It answers live from HydraDB Cloud: every answer carries source_state 'live' and a measured time, and /judge asks six questions on load with no account.
claims.caveat: This described the deployment as answering from a recorded snapshot, which was true of an earlier build and stopped being true when the cloud source landed. Production now fetches deterministic addressed records from HydraDB Cloud and Lacuna performs temporal and relationship resolution in application code. The self-hosted native Cypher path remains separate proof. The snapshot still exists under npm run serve:snapshot and is not what the deployment runs.

claims.claim: Writes to the local store stop working after enough of them, and the only remedy found is to move the store aside and reload.

measured.node_log: object store error: Operation put_opts with mode PutMode::Update not yet implemented by LocalFileSystem

claims.reproduce: bash scripts/hydra-node.sh stop && mv /var/lib/lacuna/hydradb/store /var/lib/lacuna/hydradb/store.wedged-$(date +%Y%m%d) && bash scripts/hydra-node.sh start && npm run ingest
claims.caveat: The unimplemented operation is now observed on the HTTP write path and not only in the collector loop, which is more than D-054 could say. It is still not established that the collector is what eventually kills writes, and the honest word for that is suspicion. A reset is not a fix: the replacement store runs on the same backend and should be expected to wedge again. Developing, testing and demoing are unaffected because the reset is cheap and the corpus reloads clean.

claims.claim: No credential is tracked or committed in the repository or its reachable history.
claims.why_no_data: This is a property of tracked repository content and reachable commit history, not a value any page shows.
claims.reproduce: git grep -Ein 'sk-[a-z0-9]{20}|xi-api-key|gsk_' -- . || true; git log --all -p | grep -Ein 'sk-[a-z0-9]{20}|xi-api-key|gsk_' || echo 'no committed-history hits'
claims.caveat: Ignored local environment files are outside this tracked-content claim. Two vendor keys exist in a gitignored .env.local on the author's machine and no code here reads either; they should be revoked once the submission window closes. NEEDS_VAIBHAV.md item 8.

claims.claim: The deterministic Ask path treats stored text as quoted data and never sends it to a model. The separate agent runtime is a different prompt-injection surface and is not covered by that structural guarantee.
claims.caveat: This guarantee is scoped to Ask and retrieval. Agent Context Packs contain evidence seen by a model, so their bounded prompts, no-write manifest and Reviewer stage reduce risk but do not prove that arbitrary stored instructions can never influence model output. Output escaping is a separate defence.
